newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia coffee exporters want plan with Brazil.
newsitem.headline: Colombia coffee exporters want plan with Brazil.

text.p: Colombia and Brazil should put aside traditional jealousies and develop a common coffee strategy, Colombian coffee exporters said in a report issued this week.
The National Association of Colombian Coffee Exporters (ASOEXPORT) said the two largest producers in the world should take action to avoid arabica coffees being substituted for cheaper robustas.
"Brazil and Colombia, the leaders in arabica production, should guide the future development of the sector through the policies that they establish," the ASOEXPORT report said.

The area planted with arabicas across the world dipped to 67.7 percent of the total acreage under coffee between 1995-96 compared with 71 percent in 1991-1992. At the same time the acreage of robusta crop has increased, the ASOEXPORT study said.
"Given these figures one might suggest that quality, or milder tastes, are not so decisive as they were in the past for the buyer," the report said.
ASOEXPORT said cost and price competitiveness was now uppermost in buyers' minds. Colombia has one of the highest cost per pound production costs in the coffee growing world.
In recent months tight supply fears in international markets have driven up the price of Colombian coffee to more than $2.30 per pound, its highest levels for more than two years.
That rise has also been reflected in the domestic price paid to coffee producers in Colombia, which now stands at more than 384,000 pesos (about $384) per 125-kg load.
And although arabica coffee still takes center-stage in world coffee exports, about 72 percent of the total, experts say the cheaper robustas are fast gaining ground.
"It wouldn't be surprising in the face of rapid rises in the price (of arabica) that we could end up handing over part of our market to our competitors," ASOEXPORT said.

The export organization said that the lack of coordination between Colombia and Brazil, coupled with the two countries' irrepressible desires to compete with each other could further harm prospects for the future.
"What we need is to act in a coordinated, sensible manner and try to promote the well-being of producers," ASOEXPORT said.
However, the group stopped short of recommending the formation of a new coffee cartel which it said would be contrary to the rules of the World Trade Organization.

In the case of Colombia, ASOEXPORT proposed that the National Coffee Growers' Federation should dip into its existing stockpile to meet demand rather than restrict supply with the aim of pushing up prices.
"It's not wise to ration supply in this artificial fashion in the desire to get good prices," the ASOEXPORT report said.

According to the federation's own estimates it will cut existing inventories from their current levels of about 5.0 million 60-kg bags to about 3.5 million bags by September in order to meet export schedules.
